title: Knowledge Check 11: Lessons 81-87
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 81-87 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: A candidate writes decision 4 in the scenario document: Salesforce owns the commercial shipment record and the transportation management system owns milestone events. The decision appears on the system map. Asked what the choice costs, the candidate says it costs nothing because both systems keep their existing roles. Applying the lesson's completeness test, what is the problem?
options: The decision is invalid because two systems cannot both hold shipment-related data.
The area is complete, since a decision with no cost means the choice was genuinely free.
The area is not complete: the test needs a decision, a carrier and a stated tradeoff, and a claim of zero cost usually means the cost has not been found yet.
The candidate should remove the decision from the diagram so judges cannot question it.
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the completeness test as three legs: a decision, the artifact that carries it, and the tradeoff accepted. The candidate has the first two. Saying the choice costs nothing usually means the cost is unexamined, and in this example the read-model split carries real costs in freshness and operational overhead. If a decision has no cost, the thinking is not finished.

questions.question: It is minute 130 of the 180-minute preparation. The candidate has a system map, a data model, a security model and an NFR table, but the slide deck is empty and the traceability matrix is missing rows for six secondary requirements. Which move matches the lesson's triage order?
options: Finish the six traceability rows first, then build the slides as quickly as possible.
Build the slide deck now and record the six secondary requirement rows as named gaps.
Redraw the system map with cleaner notation so the slides are faster to assemble.
Skip the consistency pass to recover the time spent on the missing rows.
questions.explanation: The lesson's cut-first list includes secondary requirements and visual polish, while the deck and the consistency pass sit in the protect-last group because the deck is the only artifact judges see during the presentation and the consistency pass catches contradictions between artifacts. Named gaps are respected; unmentioned omissions are not.

questions.question: During the 45-minute presentation, a candidate plans to show three viable architecture options and let the judges discuss which one they prefer. What does the lesson say about that approach?
options: It is correct, because letting the board choose shows collaboration and openness.
It is correct as long as each option is described in the same amount of detail.
It is a mistake: present a recommendation and frame the other options as rejected alternatives, since options without a recommendation are sloppy advisory.
It is a mistake only if the judges ask for a recommendation during the questions.
questions.explanation: The lesson quotes Salesforce's stakeholder guidance directly: providing options without recommendations is sloppy advisory. The presentation should lead with a recommendation and treat the alternatives as rejected choices with reasons, so judges spend their time testing whether the details support the recommendation.

questions.question: A candidate's Harborline Insurance draft asks for five Salesforce orgs, one per line of business, and justifies them by saying the separation keeps brokers and adjusters apart and may be needed later. Requirement isolation for brokers is already handled by external organization-wide defaults, a broker community licence, sharing sets and field-level security. Applying the lesson's accepted test for over-engineering, what is wrong with the five-org design?
options: Nothing, because separating user populations across orgs is always more secure than sharing rules.

It fails the requirement test and the rejected alternative test: no scenario requirement needs geographic isolation or recovery targets beyond platform capability, and the operational cost of synchronizing orgs lands on a team of four administrators with no developers.
It fails only because the programme window is twelve months, since multi-org is otherwise cost-neutral.
It is acceptable as long as the candidate removes the data warehouse from the same draft.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that multi-org architecture implemented just in case, without a documented business requirement justifying data synchronization, user provisioning and deployment coordination, is a documented anti-pattern. Multi-org is recommended only for recovery targets beyond platform capability, regulatory geographic isolation or full regional independence. The broker requirement is met by the sharing model, so the extra orgs serve no named requirement and carry an operating cost the client's small team absorbs.

questions.question: A candidate's NFR section reads: the renewal portal must be highly available and responsive, and everything needs 99.999 percent uptime. The platform's availability commitment is 99.9 percent. Which correction matches the lesson and the published patterns?
options: Keep the 99.999 percent target so the solution is never the weaker link, and add a note that the platform SLA applies underneath it.
Set the solution target to exactly 99.9 percent so it matches the platform commitment, then measure page load without stating a percentile.

Replace the sentence with a per-capability target, choose the availability number from the complexity ladder and state what complexity it buys, set the solution target below the platform commitment to preserve an error budget, and attach a measurement method and owner to each target.
Leave the NFR section qualitative, since the exam outline has no Non-Functional Requirements row and therefore does not score them.
questions.explanation: The lesson lists four anti-patterns here: an unmeasurable target, a uniform maximum that ignores differences in business criticality, a solution target matching the platform commitment so no error budget remains for application-layer failures, and targets set per component instead of per user-facing business capability. It also notes the outline has no NFR row, so the numbers are scored inside the areas that are listed.

questions.question: A stakeholder sends a late change during delivery: the solution shall include a new custom data object to hold vendor certifications, with an automated notification when a certification lapses. The design record already states the constraint set and one system of record per domain. Which response follows the lesson's change control rule?
options: Accept it immediately, because a written requirement outranks an architectural preference.
Refuse it and tell the stakeholder that requirements cannot be added after design begins.
Write it into the design as requested, and raise the effort in the next status report so the sponsor can see the cost.

Separate the requirement from the requested solution, price the ask in requirement, decision and cost terms, then reject it with the reason, trade it for something of equal cost, or accept it and move a named constraint in writing.
questions.explanation: The lesson's change control rule has three responses and no fourth: reject with the reason, trade for equal cost, or accept and move a constraint in writing with the sponsor named. The scenario is also the documented example of a how dressed as a what, since whether the data lives on a custom object, a standard object or a related list is the architect's call once the data shape and attributes are known.

questions.question: An architect presents a five-year case for a distribution programme. The model lists licences, implementation, operations, maintenance, integration, and change, and projects net annual value of 240,000 at run rate. A challenge comes back that the case is too optimistic. Applying the lesson's cost model, what is the most likely gap in the model?
options: The model is complete, because the six direct cost lines are the full set of costs a Salesforce solution creates.

The model omits indirect costs, which the lesson says often exceed direct costs for mature implementations: organizational costs including the opportunity cost of maintenance capacity, technical debt interest, governance overhead, and the cost of functionality that is implemented but never adopted.
The model overstates the licence line, which should always be modelled as zero because platform licences are covered by the base platform.
The model should drop maintenance, because enhancement and release adaptation fall under the implementation line as one-time cost.
questions.explanation: The lesson separates TCO into six direct lines (licence and consumption, implementation, operational, maintenance, integration, change) and four indirect categories (organizational costs, technical debt interest, governance overhead, unused functionality), and notes that indirect costs are real but easy to overlook and often exceed direct costs for mature implementations. Maintenance is described as typically consuming 60 to 80 percent of development capacity on mature solutions, so it is the largest ongoing category, not a one-time line.

questions.question: The same programme has a one-time cost of 520,000 and net annual value of 240,000 at run rate, which gives a simple payback of 2.2 years. The phased ramp shows year 1 net of negative 65,000, year 2 net of positive 185,000, and cumulative cash turning positive early in year 4, with a five-year net present value of approximately 67,000 against an undiscounted five-year net of 320,000. What does the lesson say this difference means for the architect?
options: The simple payback figure is the honest number and the ramp table should be removed from the sponsor pack, because it only creates doubt.
The gap means the discount rate should be lowered until the net present value matches the undiscounted figure, so the two numbers agree.

Steady state does not arrive on day one, most value lands in years 4 and 5 and discounting punishes that shape, so the most valuable thing the architecture can do is move value earlier; sequencing is therefore a financial instrument and each month of Phase 1 slip carries a cost of delay.
The net present value is irrelevant because payback period already accounts for the time value of money, so only the 2.2 year figure needs to be presented.
questions.explanation: The lesson shows the ramp and cumulative table precisely to make this point: the steady-state net is 240,000 a year and simple payback is 2.2 years, but cumulative cash turns positive only early in year 4 because Phase 1 delivers half a year of benefit and Phase 2 lands mid-year 2. It states that the single most valuable thing the architecture can do is move value out of year 2 and into year 1, that sequencing decides the cash curve, and that the cost of delay during the ramp is roughly 46,000 of net value per month. Payback period ignores the time value of money, which is why it flatters long programmes without the ramp shown.

questions.question: A sponsor asks two questions in the same meeting: whether the programme can be delivered cheaper, and whether it can be delivered faster. The architect has a per-month net value figure for the ramp and a named list of lower-value scope. Which pair of responses follows the lesson?
options: Answer the cost question with a promise to find savings during delivery, and answer the speed question by agreeing to compress the schedule so the sponsor stays positive about the programme.

Answer the cost question with scope rather than price by showing the specific cut, the value lines it moves, and the new payback; answer the speed question with the per-month cost of delay so acceleration becomes a decision with arithmetic attached.
Answer both questions by presenting a menu of options without a recommendation, so the sponsor chooses the tradeoff themselves.
Answer both questions by lowering the assumed value lines so the case looks more conservative, then re-present the same plan.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that the answer to cheaper is scope, not price, and that the architect should show the specific cut, the value lines it moves, and the new payback, because a sponsor who hears what a cut costs is making an informed trade. It states that the answer to faster is a cost-of-delay question, answered with the per-month value figure already calculated so the sponsor can decide rather than being managed. It also warns against presenting a menu of options without a recommendation, since that softens a recommendation into a list.

questions.question: A design review is challenged on a service account that can reach records because it runs inside the corporate network. Which principle from the security guidance settles the question?
options: Implement defense in depth.
Grant least privilege by default.
Evolve with observability.
Apply zero trust across all layers.
questions.explanation: Zero trust eliminates implicit trust based on network position or prior authentication state, so a request is verified on identity, authorization and context rather than on where it originated. In a multitenant platform the network is not a perimeter you can treat as trusted. Defense in depth and least privilege both remain relevant, but neither addresses trust granted because of origin.

questions.question: Dealers need pricing history that is too large to replicate into the org and is read only a few times a month. Which integration choice does the lesson make for that requirement?
options: Data virtualization
Batch data synchronization
Remote call in
UI update based on data changes
questions.explanation: The worked case keeps rarely read, high-volume pricing history outside the org and reads it behind an external object, and the decision guidance treats replication versus virtualization as an explicit choice per data domain. The design still owes a failure path for the virtualized read. Batch synchronization and the event patterns apply to the requirements that need local data or a UI update, not to history that stays external.

questions.question: A 900-person company with one Salesforce administrator asks which DevOps model to adopt. Following the lesson's reasoning, which model should the architect warn against buying?
options: Lean optimized
Governance optimized
Scale optimized
Full copy sandbox promotion
questions.explanation: Governance optimized release management adds approval gates and progressive exposure on top of the pipeline, and the lesson's example is that a small company buying it has purchased process it cannot staff. Each of the three models is priced against a real trade-off rather than being a maturity stage, so the decision has to be made against team size and regulatory exposure. Lean and scale optimized models cost less to operate, and a full copy sandbox is a testing environment rather than an operating model.

questions.question: An orchestrator is manipulated by a poisoned knowledge article and forwards its context to three specialists. Which control does the lesson's trust guidance prescribe at the receiving end?
options: Lower the model temperature for specialist calls
Treat inter-agent message content with the same scrutiny as external user input
Log the specialist output for monthly review
Route the request to a larger model
questions.explanation: Trust propagates through a multi-agent chain, so an orchestrator that has been manipulated passes the problem to every specialist that receives its context. The guidance is that each agent validates the context it receives before acting, because trust in the caller's identity does not mean trust in the caller's content. Logging after the fact and changing model size address output quality rather than the injection path.

questions.question: In the service desk worked example, which part of the design keeps the assistant from sending a customer response without a person involved?
options: Create task
Draft response
No send, no close, no entitlement change.
Read entitlement
questions.explanation: The tools row of the design allows reading the case, reading entitlement, creating a task and drafting a response, while the platform keeps the send, close and entitlement change capabilities out of the allowlist. Task creation is reversible and logged, which is why it is permitted. The other options are capabilities the design does grant, not limits on what the agent can do.

questions.question: A client asks which single control most reduces the damage a successful prompt injection could do. Which control does the lesson name as the highest-value one for exactly that reason?
options: Least privilege for tools.
A stop path.
Evaluation sets on every change.
Trace everything, retain deliberately.
questions.explanation: The lesson calls least privilege for tools the single highest-value control because each tool runs under a permission set sized to the action, which caps what a successful injection can achieve. A stop path limits how long an agent runs rather than what it is allowed to touch. Evaluation sets and traces detect and explain regressions, and both depend on the permission boundary being right.

questions.question: A candidate's data answer rejects extending the case object and a judge asks why the simpler option was not chosen. Which part of the lesson's answer shape is the candidate delivering?
options: The decision.
The reason tied to a requirement.
The trade-off accepted.
Integration traps.
questions.explanation: The scoring answer names the requirement the simpler option fails rather than defending complexity, which is the second part of the shape. The decision states the choice and the trade-off names what was given up with its mitigation. Integration traps is a section of the lesson rather than a component of an answer.

questions.question: An answer grants portal access through a community licence with sharing sets scoped to each dealer, but never says whether the declarative layer could express the requirement before Apex is introduced. Which trap does the lesson name for that gap?
options: No numbers.
Answering domains in isolation.
Data traps.
Declarative versus programmatic, unresolved.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that candidates should name the declarative mechanism first and justify the programmatic step only where the declarative layer cannot express the requirement. An answer that skips that justification leaves the judge unable to tell whether Apex was necessary. Omitting volumes and latency targets is a separate trap, and answering domains in isolation is about linking integration, security and data.

questions.question: Which trap does the lesson name for an answer that never states volumes, latency targets, retention periods or API limits?
options: No numbers.
Symptom instead of constraint.
Declarative versus programmatic, unresolved.
Answering domains in isolation.
questions.explanation: The lesson's trap list says volumes, latency targets, retention periods and API limits all appear in scenarios because they are meant to appear in the answer. Symptom instead of constraint is about answering with a technology rather than a chosen pattern or a sized load. The other options describe unlinked domains and an unjustified programmatic step rather than missing figures.

questions.question: A candidate has four weeks left before sitting the Platform Sharing and Visibility Architect exam and can only finish one outline section properly. The published outline weights four sections. Which one carries the most marks?
options: Permissions to standard objects, custom objects and fields
Access to Records
Access to Other Data
Implications of Security Model Choice
questions.explanation: Access to Records carries 39 percent of the exam, the single largest section in the outline, which is why the lesson treats the record access objectives as the ladder that answers most items. The permissions section carries 27 percent, Access to Other Data covers files, reports, dashboards and big objects at 16 percent, and Implications of Security Model Choice carries 18 percent. Choosing the largest section when time is short follows the weights rather than a candidate's comfort zone.

questions.question: A scenario item on the Sharing and Visibility exam describes a partner population, several hundred thousand records in the shared objects, and a bulk data load scheduled for the same weekend as go-live. The item belongs to the Implications of Security Model Choice section. Which three things must a scoring answer name?
options: The record access override, the sharing rule type, and the role hierarchy depth
The profile permissions, the permission set groups, and the login IP ranges
The scalability implications of the sharing solution, the license limitations that will impact the intended sharing solution, and how to test the sharing model
The object relationship type, the external identifier field, and the migration tool
questions.explanation: That section asks candidates to determine the scalability implications of the sharing solution, the license limitations that will impact the intended sharing solution, and how to test the sharing model. The lesson calls it the section candidates forget, and it is 18 percent of the exam. Notice that the volume figure and the concurrent bulk load in the scenario are both there to be used, because sharing recalculation over a large load is a scalability answer.

questions.question: A candidate holds Platform Developer, Platform Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect, Platform Identity and Access Management Architect and Platform Integration Architect. Which credential is granted by those four exams together?
options: Application Architect
Technical Architect
Platform Data Architect
System Architect
questions.explanation: System Architect is granted once Platform Developer, Platform Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect, Platform Identity and Access Management Architect and Platform Integration Architect are completed. Application Architect is a different set: Platform App Builder, Platform Data Architect, Platform Developer and Platform Sharing and Visibility Architect. Technical Architect sits above both, requiring the Architect Review Board Evaluation plus those two credentials.
